summary: We study how to learn an autoregressive next-token generator $f\colonΣ^\star\toΣ$ from a class $\mathcal{F}$, given chain-of-thought (CoT) demonstrations of length $T$ generated by $f$. We present a simple algorithm based on bagging, which outputs a majority vote of generators that are trained to be CoT-consistent on bootstrap samples of the training data. For binary token sets, it achieves the optimal sample complexity of $O((d_{\mathrm{VC}}+\log(1/δ))/ε)$, independent of the CoT length $T$, where $d_{\mathrm{VC}}$ is the VC dimension of $\mathcal{F}$. For finite token sets $Σ$, the VC dimension is replaced by a multiclass analogue, the Graph dimension $d_{\mathrm{G}}$, and the sample complexity is optimal up to a $\log|Σ|$ factor. The number of generators in the majority-vote ensemble is $O(\log(T/δ))$, and we show that the ensemble can be distilled into a single generator in $\mathcal{F}$ at the expense of $n\log(nT)$ unlabeled prompts.
tl_dr: We present a simple algorithm based on bagging, which outputs a majority vote of generators that are trained to be CoT-consistent on bootstrap samples of the training data.

title: Reading or Remembering? Measuring Temporal Contamination in Language Models
authors_or_owner: Arunkumar V, Gangadharan G. R., S. Senthilkumar
summary: Language models are now used to read central-bank text for economic forecasting, but most were trained on text written after the documents they read. A model reading a 2021 FOMC statement may already know that inflation rose in 2022, so part of its apparent skill can be memory of the outcome, a temporal form of test-set contamination. We measure this memory on FOMC statements and minutes from 2000 to 2026 by comparing modern open models with chronologically consistent models, which are trained only on text from before a fixed date. Asked about past GDP outcomes given only a date, models that cannot know the answer still reach an AUC of up to 0.64 from priors on dates and eras, so chance is the wrong baseline. Against these memory-free models on the same questions, most modern models recall which years had strong growth. Membership-inference scores sort documents by era and document type rather than by whether a model saw them, as exact counts in an open pretraining corpus show. In real-time nowcasts, every lookahead premium we estimate on US GDP is smaller than the forecast comparison can detect at macroeconomic sample sizes, and none on GDP or inflation survives correction for multiple testing. Lookahead audits should therefore measure memory directly against memory-free models on the same items.
tl_dr: Language models are now used to read central-bank text for economic forecasting, but most were trained on text written after the documents they read.

title: Right Reason, Wrong Advice: Evaluating Recourse in LLM Explanations of Denied Requests
authors_or_owner: Arunkumar V
summary: Language models increasingly write the explanations people receive when a rule system denies their request. If several rules deny the request independently, an explanation can name a true reason and still leave the person denied after they fix it. We call the missing property recourse validity: changing what the explanation cites, without changing what was asked for, can flip the decision. We compute it exactly, and a hitting-set argument predicts from the policy alone when a correct reason fails. In six of seven rule systems ported from access control and US benefit eligibility, a single correct reason almost never gives recourse when several reasons apply. Across 20 LLMs, checks of whether the cited reasons are correct, computed or asked of an LLM judge, are close to chance at spotting this failure, as the argument predicts. A strong judge asked whether acting on the explanation would work does spot it. Stronger and reasoning models do better but still fail on many denials with four or more independent reasons. Asking for every rule helps every open model with room to improve. Explanations of eligibility decisions should be built from the decision function and judged by whether acting on them works.
tl_dr: Language models increasingly write the explanations people receive when a rule system denies their request.

title: The cost of enforcing long-run coverage: a phase transition in online conformal prediction
authors_or_owner: Yu Gui, Rina Foygel Barber, Cong Ma
summary: Consider an online prediction setting, where at each time, we are given a new feature vector and asked to provide a prediction interval or prediction set that will likely contain the corresponding response. In this setting, if the data points are i.i.d. (or more generally, exchangeable), conformal prediction provides a mechanism for building valid prediction sets around the output of any trained model, offering coverage probability $\geq 1-α$ at each time $t$. In practice, however, issues such as distribution drift, changepoints, or other challenges may cause violations of the i.i.d. assumption. In this adversarial setting, online conformal prediction methods can still offer guarantees on long-run empirical coverage. However, there is a trade-off between these two types of goals: enforcing tight constraints on long-run empirical coverage to protect against the adversarial setting can lead to unstable oscillations in the instantaneous training-conditional coverage in the i.i.d. setting. In this work, we seek best-of-both-worlds algorithms that aim to minimize cumulative error in instantaneous training-conditional coverage when in the i.i.d. setting, while also offering long-run empirical coverage guarantees in the adversarial setting. Specifically, consider a condition that requires long-run empirical coverage to deviate from the target level $1-α$ by at most $\mathcal{O}(T^{-β})$, for some $β\in$. We prove that this family of conditions can be described with a phase transition. For $β\in[0,\frac{1}{2}]$, it is possible to construct algorithms satisfying such a constraint in the adversarial setting, while offering the same instantaneous coverage performance as split conformal prediction if the data is in fact i.i.d. On the other hand, for $β\in(\frac{1}{2},1]$, this type of condition comes at a cost, and does not achieve best-of-both-worlds behavior.
tl_dr: In this work, we seek best-of-both-worlds algorithms that aim to minimize cumulative error in instantaneous training-conditional coverage when in the i.

title: Seen but Unsaid: Locating and Repairing Cross-Image Comparison in Vision-Language Models
authors_or_owner: Zhaoning Zhang
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) often fail to match a point or an object across two images, even when the answer can be decoded from their own hidden states. We trace this failure from the visual tokens to the answer letter, in Qwen3-VL (2B-32B), InternVL3.5-8B, and Gemma-3-12B, on synthetic shape matching, same-instance point correspondence (HPatches), and semantic correspondence (SPair-71k), and find two distinct failure points, a small set of attention heads that carries the comparison, and a repair that touches 0.02% of the parameters. Two failure points: exact copies are compared but not read out. An answer-position probe exceeds the calibrated output by 15 to 25 points in every family, for nameable and unnameable shapes alike, and steering along the probe's direction moves no more answers than random directions. Semantic correspondences are present in the visual tokens but never reach the answer. One pathway: redistributing the cross-image attention of 16-32 heads, with its mass preserved, removes 17-22 points of synthetic and 15-32 points of HPatches accuracy, against at most 7 for random or attention-matched heads. A lever that training finds on its own: training only these heads' query and key projections raises SPair-71k accuracy by 28.3 points (Qwen3-VL-8B) and 25.1 points (InternVL3.5-8B), beats both layer-matched and attention-matched heads, and transfers to HPatches and BLINK. An unconstrained all-layer adapter routes 21-51% of its gain through the attention of the same heads, against at most 7% for random heads, and does so by changing what they read (83-86% of the effect) rather than their weights. Every decision rule was frozen before its run, and every reported number is recomputed by independent verification scripts.
tl_dr: Vision-language models (VLMs) often fail to match a point or an object across two images, even when the answer can be decoded from their own hidden states.

title: What Does a Bias Head Measure? Non-Identifiability in Head-Level Bias Attribution
authors_or_owner: S. M Seefat Alam
summary: Methods that localise social bias in large language models to individual attention heads and remove it by ablation are validated by their effect on a fairness metric, never by evidence that the statistic selecting the heads measures bias. We audit this on Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. The head map correlates at $ρ= -0.950$ and $-0.768$ with a label-blind response-length map, apparently identifying a surface confound. An intervention that breaks the length-label coupling rejects this reading: with the prompt held fixed, response length explains 1% of the statistic's variance. What does explain it is prompt identity, at 64% of variance, in an ordering that is not monotonic in length. Within any fixed prompt the fairness label, response length and the presence of a protected-group token are collinear at $φ= 0.95$, partly by definition of the labelling rule, so no observational analysis can attribute the map to any of them, and no method in this family performs an experiment that could. The substantive claims fail independently: bias selectivity is not late-layer-concentrated on either model under either reference reading, and no head set we tested reduces the unfairness rate when ablated. Its complement, scored on the opposite label, reliably destroys refusal behaviour ($p = 2.7\times10^{-5}$), demonstrating that the pipeline detects effects at this scale.
tl_dr: Methods that localise social bias in large language models to individual attention heads and remove it by ablation are validated by their effect on a fairness m...

title: Higher-Scoring Coding Models Did Not Get More Work Done
authors_or_owner: Yining Hua
summary: New coding models advertise themselves on score improvements of coding benchmarks. Yet no study has tested if a model that scores higher on these benchmarks gets more real work done. On June 12, 2026, a U.S. export control directive banned access to Claude Fable 5 for 19 days, which forced users to switch to other models. During this time, most former Fable 5 users switched to Opus 4.8 (11 points lower on SWE-Bench Pro compared to Fable 5). We treat this suspension as a natural experiment, where the people and projects stayed the same and only the model changed, so we could isolate the effect of Fable 5 on user productivity. We tracked GitHub pull requests of 297 Fable 5 users before, during, and after the suspension. We used 8,908 developers who stayed on Opus 4.8 all the time as the control group. We also repeated the comparison across five model upgrades before and after the suspension in 2026 (1,208 developers, 15,442 pull requests). Fitting a difference-in-differences model with developer and date fixed effects, we found that having access to Fable 5 increased the 7-day merge rate of pull requests by only 1.4 percentage points [-1.4; +4.3], which was not statistically significant. Similarly, no significant increases of merge rates were found with the upgrades (weighted mean: -0.9 percentage points [-1.9; +0.2]); all five estimates were negative (95% intervals included 0, did not differ from each other). We also did not observe a significant increase in the number of pull requests merged per week (+2.4% [-4.9%; +10.2%]).
tl_dr: New coding models advertise themselves on score improvements of coding benchmarks.

title: Feedback-Linearised Trajectory Tracking via Model-Informed Robust Geometric DDPC
authors_or_owner: Pranav Gupta, Deepan Muthirayan, Ravi Banavar
summary: Data-driven predictive control (DDPC) predicts system responses from recorded trajectories, but nonlinear dynamics can limit the accuracy of fixed linear predictors. This paper studies geometric robust DDPC for trajectory tracking of a fully actuated manipulator using model-based feedback linearisation. A mechanical model maps virtual acceleration commands into joint torques, while recorded data capture residual dynamics arising from imperfect model parameters. The controller minimises worst-case prediction error over an open Grassmannian ball centred at the fitted trajectory subspace. Simulations on a planar 2R manipulator under gravity compare the proposed method with double-integrator model predictive control (MPC) and direct regularised data-enabled predictive control (DeePC). Results show improved tracking over double-integrator MPC despite increased torque effort, while performance relative to DeePC depends on the reference trajectory.
tl_dr: Data-driven predictive control (DDPC) predicts system responses from recorded trajectories, but nonlinear dynamics can limit the accuracy of fixed linear predic...

title: Monoculture Robust Learning
authors_or_owner: Lee Cohen, Jon Kleinberg, Omer Reingold
summary: We introduce a notion of monoculture robustness in Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learning, as a way to mitigate the problem of algorithmic monoculture (Kleinberg and Raghavan, 2021): the tendency of models sharing the same components (e.g., training data) to fail on the same inputs. Specifically, we ask whether a learner with access to a single dataset can output $k$ individually accurate hypotheses whose joint failure probability is comparable to training on $k$ independent datasets. We say that such a learning procedure achieves monoculture robustness, and we quantify this by bounding the conjunctive error that all $k$ hypotheses misclassify points in an individual sense. We design methods for achieving this type of guarantee by drawing a surprising connection between replicability (Impagliazzo et al., 2022) and monoculture robustness. Specifically, we show that if the base learner is $ρ$-replicable, then running it independently $k$ times on the same sample yields individual monoculture error that shrinks exponentially with $k$, controlled by the single-run error of the base learner at the point and $ρ$. We complement these positive results with a lower bound: for individual monoculture robustness, we prove a worst-case lower bound showing that, for learners, driving the individual conjunctive error down to $γ$ can require a sample-size multiplier of $t = Ω(\log(1/γ))$.
tl_dr: We introduce a notion of monoculture robustness in Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learning, as a way to mitigate the problem of algorithmic monoculture (K...

title: PlayCraft: Designing Engaging Games from Agent Play Experience
authors_or_owner: Weihao Cheng
summary: Recent AI agents can generate playable games, but these games are not necessarily engaging. Mastery is a key source of engagement, yet designing for it requires extensive human play and tuning. We propose PlayCraft, an automated framework that uses a vision-based agent to play games and draws on its detailed play experience to revise them for mastery. Starting from an initial game, PlayCraft alternates between playing and crafting. In the playing stage, a player agent watches the game screen, uses the controls, and pursues the game objective over repeated episodes while retaining memory. After each episode, it reports its progress, outcomes, decisions, and reflections. In the crafting stage, a crafter agent uses these reports to revise the game. It estimates player abilities, predicts performance at different proficiency levels, and compares those predictions with a target learning progression. It diagnoses the game and addresses the gaps by giving players meaningful opportunities to improve through better decisions and execution. We evaluate games in fresh runs with player agents across three intelligence settings, measuring learning gain and learning slope. Compared with the initial games, PlayCraft yields larger learning gains and steeper learning slopes in most games. It also outperforms the baselines on the macro-average of each metric at every intelligence setting.
tl_dr: We propose PlayCraft, an automated framework that uses a vision-based agent to play games and draws on its detailed play experience to revise them for mastery.

title: PGX: Physically Grounded Execution for Long-Horizon Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
authors_or_owner: Kai Lu, Chenyang Ma, Ioannis Havoutis
summary: Robotic vision-language-action (VLA) models can execute diverse individual manipulation skills, yet they still struggle with long-horizon loco-manipulation tasks, where temporal structure, skills, and precision are tightly coupled within a monolithic model. We propose Physically Grounded Execution (PGX), a framework that offloads temporal and precision control to two classical training-free components, allowing the VLA to focus on stage-specific skill dynamics. PGX decomposes long-horizon loco-manipulation into three layers: (i) a predicate-based state machine governs task progression, using physical predicates to gate phase transitions, trigger recovery, and coordinate navigation and waiting. Shared predicate semantics connect offline demonstration segmentation, online execution, and stage-wise evaluation; (ii) VLA skills operate within active manipulation phases, with flat or stage-trained models concentrating on task-relevant actions; and (iii) world-coordinate locking (WCL) maintains spatial consistency through base station keeping, object-relative positioning, and world-anchored contact targets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PGX with extensive experiments conducted on three simulated tasks and one real-world task using a Unitree G1 humanoid robot for long-horizon loco-manipulation, showing improvements in stage progression and task success rates. Project page is available at: https://kl-research.github.io/pgx
tl_dr: Robotic vision-language-action (VLA) models can execute diverse individual manipulation skills, yet they still struggle with long-horizon loco-manipulation task...

title: Interactive Semi-Parametric On-Track Learning for Vehicle Dynamics in Autonomous Racing
authors_or_owner: Jungbin Kim, Youngim Nam, Cheolhyeon Kwon
summary: Autonomous racing requires an accurate vehicle dynamics model near the limits of handling, yet a mismatch between the nominal and actual dynamics inevitably remains. To reduce this mismatch, existing methods learn from on-track data, i.e., data collected while the vehicle drives on the track under racing conditions, by adapting the physical parameters of the nominal model or by learning a residual that captures the remaining mismatch. However, these on-track learning methods typically handle either the physical parameters or the residual separately, which restricts their ability to resolve the mismatch. To address this limitation, we propose an interactive semi-parametric learning framework that learns both the physical parameters and the residual under a single shared prediction-error objective. Since updating one changes the learning target of the other, they are recursively updated in turn, each guided by the other's latest update. Each update is then accepted only if it does not increase the shared objective, so that the objective is guaranteed to be non-increasing and convergent over the recursion. Numerical simulations and hardware experiments show that the proposed framework outperforms the baselines. Compared with the nominal model, it reduces the one-step prediction errors of lateral velocity and yaw rate by 90.0% and 81.6% in simulation and by 54.0% and 59.4% on hardware.
tl_dr: we propose an interactive semi-parametric learning framework that learns both the physical parameters and the residual under a single shared prediction-error objective.

title: DiTraR: Diverse Scorers and Transcript-Guided Re-ranking for Video Corpus Moment Retrieval
authors_or_owner: Mohammad Alijanpour Shalmani, Alale Rezvani Boroujeni, Ali Amini
summary: Video corpus moment retrieval asks a system to find, in a large collection of untrimmed videos with subtitles, the video and the time interval that a natural-language query describes. We find that most top-ranked errors of a strong corpus-level scorer come from choosing the wrong video, not from imprecise boundaries, and that re-weighting the evidence the scorer already uses does not fix them. We present DiTraR, which addresses video selection from two complementary directions. A witness-interval scorer decomposes the query into probes and scores every candidate interval of every corpus video exactly; a multi-scorer energy ensemble averages the energies of independently trained scorers before one exhaustive search; and a transcript verifier, a frozen language model that reads the time-stamped dialogue of the highest-ranked videos, re-orders the moments without changing their boundaries. With all settings frozen on development data and a single evaluation, DiTraR reaches 24.36 and 13.55 R@1 at IoU 0.5 and 0.7 on the TVR validation split. The ensemble improves queries about visual content, the verifier improves queries about dialogue, and their gains largely add up.
tl_dr: We present DiTraR, which addresses video selection from two complementary directions.

title: ESSI: Computationally Efficient Semantic Search for Sparse Autoencoder Concepts
authors_or_owner: James Baker
summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose diffusion model activations into interpretable features, but steering a model with them requires identifying which features map to a given semantic concept, if any. Existing methods for this concept to feature task are expensive, relying on grid searches or repeated passes through the frozen UNet. We propose Efficient Semantic Sparse Identification (ESSI). Using segmentation masks to label SDXL activations as concept or non-concept, ESSI ranks SAE features and binary-searches for the smallest set on which a linear classifier still separates positive from negative samples while not falling below a performance threshold, then reuses that classifier to calibrate the steering strength. We evaluate the same selected features on both concept insertion and object unlearning. Compared with prior work, ESSI is as cheap or cheaper, and performs well on both insertion and removal.
tl_dr: We propose Efficient Semantic Sparse Identification (ESSI).

title: FairITR: Fairness-Aware Learning of Multicategory Individualized Treatment Rules
authors_or_owner: Zeyu Chen, Wei Qian, Bintong Chen
summary: Individualized treatment rules (ITRs) recommend treatment decisions based on individual characteristics and can improve treatment outcomes beyond traditional one-size-fits-all strategies. However, similar to other commonly used algorithmic decision-making methods, ITRs without considering model fairness may result in unfair decisions across groups defined by sensitive attributes, such as race or gender. Although extensive methods have been developed for ITR estimation, most focus solely on optimizing treatment outcomes, while research on fairness-aware ITRs remains limited. Moreover, the practical scenario of multicategory treatments is rarely considered in existing fair ITR studies. To address these gaps, we introduce a fairness notion for multicategory ITRs that requires treatment decisions to be independent of sensitive attributes, and then formulate the corresponding problem of estimating fair ITRs. To solve this problem, we further propose FairITR, a fairness-aware learning framework that jointly optimizes treatment outcomes and fairness. FairITR builds on angle-based classification for multicategory ITR learning and integrates adversarial learning with covariance-based regularization to mitigate unfairness in treatment decisions. A theoretical justification for the fairness properties induced by the adversarial debiasing mechanism is also provided. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets show that FairITR substantially reduces unfairness in ITRs while maintaining competitive treatment values relative to existing baselines.
tl_dr: Individualized treatment rules (ITRs) recommend treatment decisions based on individual characteristics and can improve treatment outcomes beyond traditional on...

title: FlashAttention-4: Sub-Warp Micro-Tiling and Asynchronous Tensor Memory Acceleration
authors_or_owner: Tri Dao, Albert Gu, et al.
summary: FlashAttention-4 achieves 93% theoretical FLOPS utilization on modern Blackwell and Hopper architectures by redesigning shared memory banking patterns and overlapping systolic MMA operations with asynchronous register loads.
tl_dr: Pushes attention kernel efficiency to 93% GPU utilization with sub-warp scheduling and zero memory overhead.

title: A Bias in Disguise: Tiny Gradient Edits Stop a Small Language Model's Thinking Loops and Complement a Frontier Model's Weight Edit
authors_or_owner: Hussamuddin Syed
summary: Qwen3.5-0.8B rarely finishes reasoning in thinking mode: at a 4,096-token budget only 1 or 2 of 500 MATH-500 answers close their think block (two seeds), and accuracy is 15.4%. A recent demonstration had GPT-6 Astra edit 131,072 of the model's weights without gradients and reported MATH-500 rising from 7.9% to 48.1% at a 32,768-token budget. We provide the missing gradient baseline, then combine the two edits. Fine-tuning only the 140 to 139,750 weights with the largest gradient, on the model's own correct answers to MATH training problems, raises thinking-mode MATH-500 at 4k tokens to 39.0-45.5% after 2-9 minutes of training on one GPU; 50 training examples suffice, and 1,398 random positions give only 16.3%. The gradient concentrates the edit on the most nearly constant channel of each of the first three layers. Because the model has no bias terms, an edit confined to those channels acts as a constant vector added to the residual stream: adding three fixed vectors to the unedited model matches the accuracy of such an edit. Under the Astra protocol (32k tokens, presence penalty 1.5), the Astra edit scores 52.1% (finished and correct) in our reproduction and our full-strength edits reach 45.6-45.7%, but ours win at every budget up to 16k tokens (39.5% against 6.7% at 4k). The two edits are complementary. The Astra edit plus our 139,750-weight edit at half strength scores 62.2% at 32k, 10 points above the Astra edit alone (p = 3e-9), with half as many tokens; our half-strength edit alone scores 46.7%.
tl_dr: Qwen3.5-0.8B rarely finishes reasoning in thinking mode: at a 4,096-token budget only 1 or 2 of 500 MATH-500 answers close their think block (two seeds), and ac...

title: Uncertainty-Aware Candidate Generation for Entity Linking in Cyber Threat Intelligence
authors_or_owner: Nasser Alkhulaifi, Direnc Pekaslan, Christian Wagner
summary: Entity Resolution (ER) pipelines often collapse ambiguity into early hard decisions: upstream Named Entity Recognition (NER) selects a single span and type, and downstream Entity Linking (EL) treats that choice as ground truth. This discards valuable information about the ambiguity of the underlying data (e.g., span boundary disagreement and type confusion), leading to brittle systems that fail unpredictably when faced with uncertainty in inputs. Therefore, this work presents a proof-of-concept for uncertainty-aware ER that treats uncertainty as native data that should be preserved and exploited throughout ER pipelines. We (i) capture uncertainty signals in the NER stage and (ii) leverage these signals into the EL stage to improve candidate retrieval under ambiguity. Using a BERT-based NER model augmented with two auxiliary span-boundary prediction heads, we apply Monte Carlo (MC) dropout at inference time to derive three mention-level proxy signals: the MC-averaged start-boundary probability, the MC-averaged end-boundary probability, and De Luca-Termini fuzzy entropy computed over the Begin-Inside-Outside (BIO) predictive distribution. These signals are used to adapt the fuzzy cutoff in candidate generation (CG) for EL. Because CG is treated as a blocking step, we evaluate retrieval recall. On the AnnoCTR dataset linked to the MITRE ATTCK knowledge base, the boundary-aware and dual-signal fuzzy linking approaches improve Recall@10 from 0.6186 to 0.7966. The contribution lies not in an end-to-end optimised ER pipeline but in establishing uncertainty preservation as a viable and beneficial component of ER pipelines, enabling downstream EL to make better-informed decisions under uncertainty.
tl_dr: Entity Resolution (ER) pipelines often collapse ambiguity into early hard decisions: upstream Named Entity Recognition (NER) selects a single span and type, and...

title: Understanding Clipping In Zeroth-Order Optimization
authors_or_owner: Saket Gollapudi, Elisa Bertino, Sewoong Oh
summary: Zeroth-order optimization has emerged as a resource-efficient alternative to Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) when fine-tuning LLMs, thanks to the inherent low dimensionality of the loss landscape. It relies on a two-point estimate of the gradient that only accesses the function value and not the gradient, bypassing the resource-heavy backpropagation. Recently, it was accidentally discovered that per-sample clipping can improve the performance of the trained model, while running a differentially private version of zeroth-order optimization \cite{zhang2024dpzero} with a very large privacy parameter $ε$ (corresponding to very little privacy). In this paper, we systematically investigate this phenomenon and demonstrate that ($i$) the optimal choice of learning rate $η$ is inversely proportional to the clipping threshold $c$, satisfying $ηc =$ constant; ($ii$) clipping drives the zeroth-order optimization to a different solution with higher test accuracy; and ($iii$) this phenomenon is only observed with per-sample clipped zeroth-order optimization and not other zeroth-order alternatives that also provide robust estimates of the gradient. Further analyses with artificially injected label noise reveals that clipping leads to more robust predictions, which stems from the implicit down weighting of hard-to-fit training examples. Our code is available at https://github.com/SewoongLab/ClipZero
tl_dr: Zeroth-order optimization has emerged as a resource-efficient alternative to Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) when fine-tuning LLMs, thanks to the inherent low...

title: DynMF2: Rigid Motion Factorization by Expectation-Maximization for Monocular 4D Reconstruction and Motion Segmentation
authors_or_owner: Agelos Kratimenos, Yile Hua, Kostas Daniilidis
summary: A single casual video leaves a moving scene under-determined: a point seen once from each place can slide toward or away from the camera and still match every frame. We constrain the reconstruction with the structure of the motion itself. Building on DynMF, we model a scene's motion as a handful of SE(3) trajectories, each rigid, and let every point follow one of them alone, never a blend. DynMF2 computes this factorization directly from 3D point trajectories, with no rendering, by Expectation-Maximization (EM). Its M-step fits, in closed form, every rigid motion to the points assigned to it, and its E-step reassigns every point to the motion that explains it with the least error. The background is simply one more motion, the camera's, so no masks are needed. Three tools then revise the factorization: requery adds trajectories where the rendering shows parts the tracker missed, merge joins motions that move together, and split separates those that do not. Thus the number of motions follows the scene. Without masks, DynMF2 clearly outperforms the mask-based baselines in view synthesis on iPhone and NVIDIA and in 3D tracking on iPhone. It recovers what masks leave out, from thin parts and details to small movers far in the background. Its motions segment the moving parts of MOVi-F and iTACO scenes competitively, although DynMF2 is never trained to segment. What moves in a scene is not decided in advance: it emerges from the rigid motions themselves.
tl_dr: A single casual video leaves a moving scene under-determined: a point seen once from each place can slide toward or away from the camera and still match every f...

title: Interpretable and Accurate Hybrid Decision Trees with Selective Case-Based Splits
authors_or_owner: Cristiano Landi, Alessio Cascione, Riccardo Guidotti
summary: Decision trees are among the most well-known interpretable models in Machine Learning. Over the years, a wide variety of strategies have been proposed to define split conditions within the greedy learning framework, aiming to guide instance routing and enhance predictive performance. These strategies range from axis-parallel and oblique splits based on feature values to proximity-based splits using exemplar instances and more complex hybrid approaches. However, no single method has emerged as universally superior. In this work, we present two key contributions to the construction of greedy decision trees. First, we propose a hybrid tree architecture that integrates both feature-based and case-based splits, allowing for heterogeneous splits throughout the tree. Second, we introduce a novel type of split that leverages a selective case-based approach: when a split is needed, our method searches for the most informative subset of features to define the split, effectively balancing the specificity of case-based methods with the simplicity of feature-based ones. Experiments on a diverse set of tabular datasets show that our method outperforms standard decision trees and achieves performance on par with ensemble methods, while producing shallow trees that retain or even improve predictive accuracy.
tl_dr: we propose a hybrid tree architecture that integrates both feature-based and case-based splits, allowing for heterogeneous splits throughout the tree.

title: Shape-Aware Three-Way Merge for RDF Knowledge Graphs: The schema defines the conflict: an implementation and evaluation
authors_or_owner: Steve Brown
summary: Merging RDF serializations creates ordering conflicts and misses semantic ones. We describe and evaluate a three-way merge in which the schema defines a conflict: set algebra combines canonical triples, and a slot is contended only where a SHACL shape bounds its cardinality and both sides' changes cannot stand within that bound. Unbounded predicates union; contended slots go to a person. The same shapes graph validates the result. We do not claim the first three-way merge for RDF. Our contribution is an implementation in a production multi-agent store and an evaluation against a reimplementation of Quit Store's Context Merge overlap rule, which it extends rather than replaces, and six other strategies. Across five synthetic seeds, the shape-aware operator raised 33 conflicts, all true positives as judged by the same shapes that define them, with no triples lost or fabricated and no SHACL violations admitted. The context-overlap baseline, counted per slot, detected the same 33 conflicts but asked 845 questions. A replay built from recorded production incidents covers 105 human alias repairs (93 after excluding 12 chained pairs) and 939 duplicate-value incidents. It reproduces a triple-level limit: different names for one entity remain invisible (0 of 93 alias repairs detected, matching 0 of 21 synthetic cases). In a study of evolving shape contracts, merging shape declarations first handles the tested cardinality changes, while datatype evolution exposes a detector blind spot caught by post-merge validation. An oracle that reads no shapes agrees with the shipped operator on the facts and history of all 23 reachable single-slot cases. Under wrong shapes, a missing bound loses data silently and a spurious one only adds questions. The supported claim is fewer human decisions with nothing silently lost, for cardinality conflicts in one deployment, not general merge correctness.
tl_dr: Merging RDF serializations creates ordering conflicts and misses semantic ones. We describe and evaluate a three-way merge in which the schema defines a conflict: set algebra combi...

title: BrickFlow: Connectivity-Guided Brick Reconstruction
authors_or_owner: Peter Kulits, Cordelia Schmid
summary: Given a set of LEGO parts and an image of an assembled object, our task is to infer the pose of each part to assemble the object. In contrast with traditional 3D reconstruction, doing so requires satisfying discrete physical constraints, which provide structure but render the problem combinatorial and highly sensitive to small pose errors. To learn a prior over how parts fit together, we train a set-conditioned SE(3) flow model on procedurally generated assemblies. We then finetune this model to inject image conditioning, using 1% as much data. However, while the learned flow captures global structure, it does not enforce connectivity. To address this, we introduce an analytic connectivity-field guidance to pull predictions toward connected assemblies at test time. Through this, we demonstrate improved build quality with model size, pretraining, and guidance. We make our models and data available for research purposes at https://kulits.github.io/BrickFlow/
tl_dr: we introduce an analytic connectivity-field guidance to pull predictions toward connected assemblies at test time.

title: Linking Rapid Learning to Compositional Structure in Neural Networks: Evidence from Additive Analogies in Meta-Learned Parameter Spaces
authors_or_owner: Abigail L. Tenenbaum, R. Thomas McCoy
summary: Humans can learn rapidly from limited experience, while neural networks typically require extensive training. In this work, we investigate what properties of a neural network can enable it to learn rapidly. We study neural networks that have been optimized via meta-learning, a technique that exposes a network to many related functions to facilitate its subsequent learning of similar functions. Prior work has shown that these meta-learned networks can learn new functions rapidly, but how they do so remains unclear. To investigate their internal structure, we take inspiration from classic work demonstrating additive relationships among the learned vectors that neural networks use to represent words (e.g., "king" minus "man" plus "woman" approximates "queen"). Analogously, we look for additive relationships among a meta-learned network's "representations" of different functions; when a meta-learned network rapidly learns to implement a specific function, all of its adapted parameter values can be concatenated into a single vector that we treat as representing the function. We find that such parameter vectors can be added and subtracted according to symbolic relationships among the functions they represent, yielding new parameter vectors that successfully represent the functions predicted by the corresponding symbolic manipulations: the networks specified by these artificially recombined vectors actually implement the intended functions without any direct training on them. Our results suggest that meta-learning can tune a network's starting point to organize subsequent learning along systematic, functionally meaningful trajectories through the space of possible parameter vectors, providing a geometric basis for realizing inductive biases in neural networks.
tl_dr: In this work, we investigate what properties of a neural network can enable it to learn rapidly.

title: Combinatorial Bernoulli Factories with Polynomially Many Coins
authors_or_owner: Renato Paes Leme, Rad Niazadeh
summary: We provide an efficient implementation of combinatorial Bernoulli factories. Such a factory turns coins of unknown biases $x$ into a random vertex of a polytope $P$ whose mean is exactly $x$. For every affine slice of the cube (the class of polytopes that admit a factory), we give a single algorithm whose expected number of coin flips and running time at every interior $x$ are polynomial in the dimension and in $1/{δ_*}$, where ${δ_*}=\min_i\{x_i,1-x_i\}$ is never supplied to the algorithm. For perfect matchings this gives $O(n^{8}{δ_*}^{-2}\log(n/{δ_*}))$ flips, while the factory of Niazadeh, Paes Leme, and Schneider [STOC 2021] spends at least $n^{2n-1}$ flips in expectation at the uniform doubly stochastic matrix. For other polytopes, our method rounds exactly given a point deep inside $P$ and the promise that $x$ is far from the boundary of $P$.
tl_dr: We provide an efficient implementation of combinatorial Bernoulli factories. Such a factory turns coins of unknown biases $x$ into a random vertex of a polytope $P$ whose mean is e...

title: BAL: Bidirectional Autoregression in Latent Space for Learning Human Movement Representations
authors_or_owner: Genki Kinoshita, Ko Nishino
summary: Learning semantically meaningful human movement representations from 3D pose sequences is essential for human behavior modeling. Existing self-supervised methods derive supervision from artificial assumptions, e.g., invariance to augmentation within a certain range or recoverability of masked regions at a certain temporal scale, introducing heuristic hyperparameters that make the learned semantics sensitive to their settings. We propose BAL, a self-supervised framework that instead exploits supervision intrinsic to human movement: the natural ordering structure of everyday behavior. BAL autoregressively predicts in a semantically abstract latent space, analogous to how humans anticipate others' actions rather than their precise joint configurations. Bidirectional autoregressive prediction, both forward and backward in time, fully leverages these ordering constraints while enabling representation extraction using both past and future context at inference. To suppress representation collapse, BAL decomposes each prediction target into a global component capturing sequence-level semantics and a local component capturing context-independent movement. We prove that the local targets retain nontrivial angular diversity unless the representations are completely collapsed, preserving a meaningful training signal. Experiments on large-scale datasets demonstrate that BAL's representations are highly effective for motion captioning, forecasting, and interpolation, outperforming baselines on most evaluation metrics.
tl_dr: We propose BAL, a self-supervised framework that instead exploits supervision intrinsic to human movement: the natural ordering structure of everyday behavior.

title: DynSurvX: Time-Resolved Explanations for Dynamic Survival Predictions
authors_or_owner: Van Tuan Nguyen, Agathe Guilloux
summary: Recent survival models integrating longitudinal data achieve strong predictive performance, but their predictions are often difficult to interpret, limiting their clinical use. We propose DynSurvX, a model-agnostic explainability framework for dynamic survival prediction with mixed static and longitudinal covariates. Based on Shapley values, DynSurvX introduces a hierarchical two-phase strategy that first identifies influential longitudinal features and then adaptively refines their temporal importance, enabling fine-grained explanations while reducing computational cost. The framework provides time-resolved explanations that evolve as new patient data become available. Experiments on simulated and two clinical datasets show varying agreement with theoretical importance across prediction models, with closer agreement for better-performing models, alongside clinically interpretable insights in real-world settings. It remains robust across prediction settings and reduces computation time by 41--80\% relative to the temporal explanation baseline, making dynamic explanations practical.
tl_dr: We propose DynSurvX, a model-agnostic explainability framework for dynamic survival prediction with mixed static and longitudinal covariates.

title: An inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient method for constrained convex finite-sum optimization
authors_or_owner: Zhaosong Lu, Yifeng Xiao
summary: In this paper, we study a class of constrained convex finite-sum optimization problems. In many practical applications, all or some of the constraints are hard constraints that represent imperative requirements. Consequently, any desirable approximate solution must (nearly) satisfy these constraints. Motivated by this, we focus on computing an $ε$-$surely\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ ($ε$-SFSO) solution, in which the constraint violation is deterministically bounded by $ε$, and the expected optimality gap is at most $ε$. While a recently proposed stochastic variance-reduced first-order penalty method can compute an $ε$-SFSO solution, there remains a significant gap between its first-order oracle complexity for computing an $ε$-SFSO solution and that for computing an $ε$-$expected\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ solution, where both the expected constraint violation and the expected optimality gap are bounded by $ε$. To narrow this gap, we propose an inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient (SVRG) method that significantly improves the previously best-known first-order oracle complexity for computing an $ε$-SFSO solution. Furthermore, when the objective consists of a single function, the proposed method reduces to a novel deterministic first-order method for solving standard convex conic optimization. It achieves a significantly lower gradient evaluation complexity with respect to the objective function compared to existing methods, and can outperform them when computing constraint gradients and projections onto the associated cone is cheaper than evaluating the objective gradient. Preliminary numerical results are presented to illustrate the performance of the proposed method.
tl_dr: In this paper, we study a class of constrained convex finite-sum optimization problems.

title: Déjà View: A Shared Working-Memory Model for Visual Tasks
authors_or_owner: Mranmay Shetty, Gabriel Kreiman
summary: A working-memory model must remember stimuli and use its memory flexibly to perform different tasks. Here we introduce a model of working memory for images that combines dynamic activity with temporary associations between image features. We train the model on five tasks, including remembering a sample while other images are presented, categorizing distractor images while remembering the sample, and determining whether an image is new or has been presented before. The same trained model performs all tasks, guided by explicit cues about which response is required. We use this flexible memory model to ask how delay, distraction, and image history affect performance. Delays have little effect on sample-memory performance for the delays we tested, while seeing more images leads to more false alarms even when the target image appeared equally recently in all cases. On the sample-memory-plus-categorization task, the probability of correct responses on all questions decreases as more questions are asked, despite robust sample-memory performance. Finally, the model maintains stable performance across 40 brief trials of each task under the tested conditions. Together, these results demonstrate how a single working-memory system can be flexibly used to perform different tasks, and how its errors depend on both previous images and task demands.
tl_dr: we introduce a model of working memory for images that combines dynamic activity with temporary associations between image features.

title: Decomposing SGD Dynamics in Neural Networks: Teacher-Induced Spikes and Variance Inflation
authors_or_owner: Samet Demir, Zafer Dogan
summary: We study two-layer neural networks trained by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on a multi-index teacher model, focusing on how first-layer parameters orthogonal to the teacher subspace affect generalization. We decompose the first-layer weights into a signal component aligned with the teacher and an orthogonal complement, and analyze their joint SGD dynamics together with the second layer in the proportional limit. We show that although SGD updates to the complement are initially isotropic, the training dynamics induce teacher-dependent spectral spikes in the complement Gram matrix. This emergent anisotropy provides a concrete mechanism by which representation variance is amplified, and generalization degrades. To isolate this effect, we introduce Decomposed Dynamics, an analytically tractable surrogate whose asymptotic test-error dynamics coincide with those of SGD. In simulations with a ReLU student, freezing the directions of the orthogonal complement improves generalization relative to training them. Finally, we show that the signal component rapidly aligns with the second-layer weights, revealing strong cross-layer coupling even in this shallow setting. Together, our results provide a dynamical explanation for how feature learning outside the teacher subspace harms generalization.
tl_dr: we introduce Decomposed Dynamics, an analytically tractable surrogate whose asymptotic test-error dynamics coincide with those of SGD.

title: Equivariant Modeling with Polynomial Features via Minimal Homogeneous Generators
authors_or_owner: Michael Liaofan Liu, Joe Kileel
summary: We present a general framework for modeling and learning equivariant functions between finite dimensional semisimple real group representations, unifying constructions developed across many application areas. Our model is a linear combination of equivariant polynomial features whose coefficients are arbitrary learnable functions of invariant polynomial features. We take as features minimal homogeneous generators for the invariant algebra and the covariant module over the invariant algebra, up to prescribed degrees. We provide a Python package that automatically computes these features and fits the resulting models to training data. The algorithm for feature computation requires explicit isotypic decompositions of the input and output representations, along with explicit Clebsch-Gordan decompositions of the tensor product of irreducible representations, and achieves speedups over alternative methods in computational algebra. Numerical experiments in scientific modeling demonstrate the full learning pipeline and yield accurate predictors with few trainable parameters, using the model both for end-to-end prediction and within layers of larger architectures.
tl_dr: We present a general framework for modeling and learning equivariant functions between finite dimensional semisimple real group representations, unifying constr...

title: Auditing black-box clinical prediction models with a large language model through queries alone: a blinded test with planted flaws
authors_or_owner: Zhiyu Liu, Xinyu Yang
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are used to explain clinical prediction models, on the promise that they can say what a model computes, find its faults and even reveal new knowledge in it. We tested the three promises where the answers could be checked. From the International Stroke Trial we trained four kinds of model (logistic regression, explainable boosting machine, gradient-boosted trees, neural network) for two outcomes on patients randomised earlier, planted one flaw in each of 24 copies (an under-predicted subgroup, a reversed risk factor or an implausible step) and mixed them with the 8 clean models. GPT-6 Astra audited each model three times, blind, through a tool that only returned the model's predictions; the judging rules were committed before any run and applied by program. Its surrogate models, with a median of 128 terms, reproduced the audited models' log-odds with a mean $R^2$ of 0.976 (0.959 for an additive surrogate of 42 terms fitted by an analyst). It found the planted flaw in 69 of 72 runs (96%; 95% CI 80% to 99%); a script written for the purpose found all 24. It also reported many more problems: 60% of 1,089 checkable reports failed the pre-specified check against the model's average behaviour; post hoc, most of these were real but small steps, and 15% of the checkable reports were not found in the model. Of 601 unexpected relationships it read out of the clean models, 11% held in patients randomised later (random pairs 6%; a regression scan's shorter list of its strongest candidates, 28%); after a check on the training data, 33% against 30%. With query access alone, an LLM can describe a black-box model faithfully and find nearly every planted flaw, as a purpose-written script also did; its reports of problems must be checked on the model and its discoveries on data.
tl_dr: Large language models (LLMs) are used to explain clinical prediction models, on the promise that they can say what a model computes, find its faults and even re...

title: General progress substitutes for specific training data in language models
authors_or_owner: Mark Marosi, Peter Antal
summary: Language models acquire their capabilities from training data, and developers withhold data during training to keep models from learning capabilities that could be misused. How long this delays a capability, and how much data is needed to acquire it later, is unknown. Here we show that the general progress a model makes on the rest of its training data substitutes for the data that was withheld. We withheld the training signal for individual skills in models of chess, Othello, molecular strings, bracket languages and web text. The delay of a withheld skill in larger models was predicted from smaller ones. A chess model never explicitly trained to respond to check ranked the legal responses almost as well as a model that was. When models were then trained on the withheld data, they acquired the skill with a small fraction of the data needed from initialization, and this fraction decreased as the models progressed. A control rule of equal difficulty was learned much more slowly. A programming language withheld from the training text of a 7-billion-parameter model was regained in the same way. Data filtering therefore delays a capability, and the data required to regain it decreases as models improve.
tl_dr: we show that the general progress a model makes on the rest of its training data substitutes for the data that was withheld.

title: Simple Private Noisy SGD is Minimax-Optimal under Population Strong Convexity
authors_or_owner: Valentin Roth, Marco Avella Medina
summary: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is at the center of modern machine learning and is known to be statistically minimax-optimal in many regression settings, e.g., for convex Generalized Linear Models (GLMs). Yet, it is unknown whether its simplest differentially private Noisy SGD counterpart fulfills similar favorable guarantees even on strongly convex losses. We resolve this question affirmatively. We upper bound the parameter estimation error for a single pass of Noisy SGD with a fixed stepsize schedule and constant batch sizes on smooth and strongly convex Lipschitz losses over a compact convex domain under Renyi DP. Specialized to strongly convex GLMs, our error bounds match minimax lower bounds we derive based on the Score Attack framework. In particular, this provides the first minimax-optimal rate for Noisy SGD in private logistic regression, avoiding poly-logarithmic terms present in existing results. Our analysis is versatile as it relies on standard convex analysis and establishes the same rates in expectation and with high probability.
tl_dr: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is at the center of modern machine learning and is known to be statistically minimax-optimal in many regression settings, e.g....

title: What Must a Model Tell a Planner? Outcome Interfaces for Risk-Aware Planning After Robot Damage
authors_or_owner: Hassan Iqbal, Krishna Kumar
summary: When a robot is damaged, it must decide which routes it can still afford, and the amount of risk it may accept can change from one mission to the next. We argue that whether a learned model helps such a robot depends on its decision interface, that is, on what the model hands to the planner. A decision policy tells the planner what to do, whereas an outcome model, a kind of world model, predicts the consequences of each route. We study simulated Unitree Go2 quadrupeds and H1 humanoids with weakened motors, added payloads, or reduced foot friction. We compare four interfaces. The first is a decision policy, and the second is the same policy trained with fixed penalties for infeasible routes. The third is an outcome model that predicts the feasibility and travel time of each route. The fourth, which we call a capability contract, is an outcome model that predicts the chance of success and the travel time of the robot on each terrain and composes them along a route. All share the same collected experience, matched tuning and risk calibration, and an uncertainty guard. Two comparatively low-risk probes let the capability contract rank hazardous terrains about as well as four new trials on every hazard. At a calibrated 5% limit on selecting empirically infeasible routes, outcome models cut declined missions from about 32% to 7-8% on Go2 and from 57% to 35-36% on H1 compared with the plain policy. Fixed penalties narrow this gap, but the best penalty changes with the risk target. Predicting outcomes lets the planner preserve missions by changing routes as risk requirements tighten.
tl_dr: When a robot is damaged, it must decide which routes it can still afford, and the amount of risk it may accept can change from one mission to the next.

title: Spectrum Adaptation of AI-Native Autoencoder Communications with Transfer Learning
authors_or_owner: Yalin E. Sagduyu, Tugba Erpek
summary: End-to-end physical-layer learning replaces separate modulation, coding, and detection operations with an autoencoder (AE) that consists of a jointly trained encoder-decoder pair at the transmitter and the receiver. This paper studies AI-native communications with AEs and quantifies the sensitivity to training-test mismatch in channel models. Models trained only on an AWGN channel achieve low bit error rates (BERs) under matched conditions but degrade severely on Rayleigh fading with practical front-end impairments. To reduce the time and energy required to adapt to new channel conditions, we propose a low-latency transfer-learning procedure that starts from an AWGN-pretrained system and fine-tunes only a small subset of transmitter and receiver layers while freezing the remainder. We further formulate layer selection as a budget-constrained optimization problem that identifies the most informative parameters to update during adaptation. This preserves the learned signal geometry and the deep decision structure while adapting lightweight front ends to fading- and impairment-induced mixing. For AE communications, we show that partial updates remove the mismatch-induced error floor and approach the BER of fully retrained models. We provide a layer-wise study and quantify resource-performance trade-offs, showing that modest adaptation substantially reduces BER while cutting training time, multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations, energy consumption, and the fraction of updated parameters for resource-efficient implementation.
tl_dr: we show that partial updates remove the mismatch-induced error floor and approach the BER of fully retrained models.

title: Sliding-Window Detection of Hidden Regimes under Stochastic Switching
authors_or_owner: Arina Pambukyan, Hayk Nersisyan
summary: A sliding-window average is a simple estimator of the current state of a hidden regime-switching process, such as a hidden Markov model. A longer window averages out more noise but is more likely to contain a switch, and the question is what such a switch costs. We analyse the decoder that assigns the average of the last $m$ observations to the nearest regime mean. For two regimes with conditionally independent, stochastically ordered observations, a switch inside the window, averaged uniformly over its positions and directions, causes an error with probability exactly $1/2$. Consequently, for every stationary switching law, the error is at most $\bar P(m)+\bar s(m-1)/2$, where $\bar P(m)$ is the stationary-weighted single-regime error and $\bar s$ the switch rate. Under Markov switching, time reversal shows that a window whose oldest and current regimes differ is misclassified with probability exactly $1/2$, however many switches it contains, and the bound is attained up to a factor $p_{\min}^{m-1}$. For Gaussian noise with common variance, minimizing the bound gives an explicit window length which, in units of $σ^2/Δ^2$, depends only on the expected number of switches in that time. As switching probabilities vanish proportionally, the optimal error is $\bar s\log(1/\bar s)/(2I)(1+o(1))$, with $I$ the single-regime Chernoff exponent. In the Gaussian case this is twice the Bayes error. For symmetric switching, exponentially weighted moving averages reduce this factor to at most $2\log2\approx1.39$, and two-block weights adapted to the switch rate attain the Bayes rate. For three or more regimes, long-window switch costs are set by the geometry of the regime means. For Markov-modulated random walks with $\pm1$ steps on a reflecting lattice, a position-aware decoder learns as fast as without walls under holding boundaries, while steps at bouncing boundaries carry none.
tl_dr: A sliding-window average is a simple estimator of the current state of a hidden regime-switching process, such as a hidden Markov model.

title: Linear Regression with Self-Selection Bias in Polynomial Time
authors_or_owner: Felix Zhou
summary: We revisit the problem of estimating $k$ linear regressors with self-selection bias in $n$ dimensions up to error $\varepsilon$ with the maximum self-selection criterion, as introduced by Cherapanamjeri, Daskalakis, Ilyas, and Zampetakis [CDIZ23, STOC]. Our main result is a $\mathrm{poly}(n,k,1/\varepsilon)$ time algorithm for the unknown-index variant of this problem, thereby improving upon the running times of the best known algorithms due to Gaitonde and Mossel [GM24] and Kalavasis, Mehrotra, and Zhou [KMZ26, COLT] with exponential dependence on $k$. Our algorithm succeeds in the presence of correlated noise between regressors, which captures the related setting of max-affine regression. Consequently, we also give the first polynomial-time algorithm for this problem, improving on the prior works of Ghosh, Pananjady, Guntuboyina, and Ramchandran [GPGR22, IEEE Transactions on Information Theory] and Gaitonde and Mossel [GM24] with exponential dependence on $k$. Prior works exhaustively search over a $k$-dimensional subspace spanned by the regressors, using conditional moments of the response to test candidates. In contrast, our algorithm is driven by an improved understanding of the moments of the covariates. We show that, restricting to observations with large response values, the degree-$(\log n)$ Hermite moment of the covariates approximately decomposes as a sum of tensor powers of the regressors. The first step of our algorithm can be viewed as a tensor decomposition algorithm for these implicitly represented high-order tensors, which outputs unit vectors parallel to the regressors. A secondary step based on a simple variant of ordinary least squares extracts estimates for the regressors given these unit vectors. We believe our analytic insight and algorithmic components may have applications to designing efficient algorithms for other latent-variable problems.
tl_dr: We revisit the problem of estimating $k$ linear regressors with self-selection bias in $n$ dimensions up to error $\varepsilon$ with the maximum self-selection ...

title: Why Finite Intelligence Works in an Infinite World: A Mathematical Theory
authors_or_owner: Mojtaba Soltanalian
summary: An information system often has to learn before it knows what it will be asked. A finite representation can succeed without recording an infinite environment in full when those asks share collective structure, rather than demand unrelated facts scattered arbitrarily across it. We formalize this phenomenon through future-task information, the minimum retained information needed to preserve decision value relative to the available evidence. A joint decision-regret state records posterior comparisons among actions for every permitted task. Under compactness assumptions, every retained representation admits a calibrated replacement based on this state, preserving all task regrets without increasing information; the resulting information-regret curve equals an operational coding rate. Two exact boundaries govern finite preservation: weak-star closure for a fixed action count, and the singular mass of the source-evidence law when all finite action menus are admitted. Collective structure determines information requirements beyond individual-question difficulty. Families with identical source laws, pairwise task metrics, and individual-task rates can have different high-resolution exponents. Covariance-identical coordinate and parity families have different exact rate-distortion curves, with optimal parity retention characterized by a sharp Fourier-entropy inequality. For balanced nested task families, refinement sizes and weighted reach determine the rate within an additive constant, attained by prefix coding under explicit decay conditions. Nonlinear learning and computational separations distinguish preservation from efficient discovery and use. The proposed mathematical theory identifies which shared decision requirements allow finite information to remain useful for infinitely many possible purposes.
tl_dr: An information system often has to learn before it knows what it will be asked. A finite representation can succeed without recording an infinite environment in full when those ask...

title: Asymptotic Margins and Feature Confinement in Conic Classification Heads under Softmax Cross-Entropy
authors_or_owner: Omer Nezih Gerek
summary: Classification heads built on conic functions give each class a bounded region of the feature space, and such regions are used to reject samples of unseen classes. We ask whether these regions also keep the features bounded when the head is trained with softmax cross-entropy. For a head whose class scores combine a linear term with a Euclidean norm, we first show that the region of each class is bounded by a quadric of revolution, whose eccentricity is the reciprocal of one learned ratio. We then attach to each class an asymptotic margin, which compares the growth of its score with the growth of all the other scores and can be computed by a second-order cone program. The loss of a class has infimum zero exactly when its margin is positive, and it then approaches zero only along diverging features. When the margin is negative, the loss is coercive and its minimizers lie in an explicit ball. Since softmax depends only on the differences between scores, a class with a bounded region can still have a positive margin, so bounded regions do not confine the features. The result extends to other norms, including the polyhedral conic functions. On CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, all 1210 cells of 67 trained conic heads have positive margins, whereas a prototype head keeps nine of its ten cells bounded, as the theory predicts.
tl_dr: Classification heads built on conic functions give each class a bounded region of the feature space, and such regions are used to reject samples of unseen class...

title: TRACE: Topological Representations for Anomaly detection through Contrastive Embeddings
authors_or_owner: Sydney Johns
summary: Intrusion detectors must recognize evolving malicious behavior even when confirmed attack labels are scarce or incomplete. We present TRACE, a topology-aware graph contrastive learning framework for label-efficient intrusion detection. TRACE learns from benign system-activity graphs by combining message-passing and topological representations, then assigns anomaly scores in the same projected embedding space optimized by the contrastive objective. This design captures both local interactions and graph-scale structural deviations without using attack labels during representation learning. A labeled validation set containing benign and malicious graphs is used only to calibrate the anomaly threshold. We evaluate TRACE on StreamSpot, GraSec-IoT, and Unicorn Wget against a supervised graph neural network and the benign-only GraphCL baseline. TRACE obtains F1 scores of 0.923, 0.790, and 0.583, respectively. Compared with GraphCL, this is higher on StreamSpot (0.450) and Unicorn Wget (0.203), but lower on GraSec-IoT (0.975). The supervised model leads on StreamSpot and GraSec-IoT, whereas TRACE has the highest F1 on Unicorn Wget. The mixed results show that topology-aware benign-only learning can improve detection in some graph settings but does not provide a uniform advantage.
tl_dr: We present TRACE, a topology-aware graph contrastive learning framework for label-efficient intrusion detection.

title: Fine-Tuning Gemma 4 Edge Models for MATLAB Signal-Processing Code with SFT and QLoRA on a Laptop iGPU
authors_or_owner: Mehmet Altan Toksöz
summary: Small language models that run on a laptop are attractive for writing signal-processing code offline, but they make systematic errors on digital signal processing (DSP) conventions. We apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to the Gemma 4 edge models E2B and E4B with 66 checked examples covering 11 signal-processing MATLAB subtasks, using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and quantized LoRA (QLoRA) on the integrated GPU (iGPU) of a laptop, and deploy the 8-bit integer (int8) models with the adapters through OpenVINO. On held-out variants scored by deterministic checkers, the pass rate rises from 18/66 to 37/66 (LoRA) and 37/66 (QLoRA) for E2B and from 32/66 to 47/66 for E4B (QLoRA). Reading all 159 failing programs shows that the adapters remove most errors of convention, such as the sign of a lag, units and array shapes, but few errors in building signals and noise. Applied at run time, the adapter costs 17-19% of the generation speed.
tl_dr: Small language models that run on a laptop are attractive for writing signal-processing code offline, but they make systematic errors on digital signal processi...

title: Fold Weighting for Cross-Validation Under Continuous Distributional Drift
authors_or_owner: Yegor Baranovski
summary: Cross-validation weights all folds equally, so under drift the oldest folds count as much as the newest. We model drift by a Hölder condition in total variation distance and give finite-sample bounds on the excess deployment risk of the configuration that sliding-window cross-validation selects. Each bound splits into drift, estimation, and validation-noise terms. With equal weights the drift terms saturate as the record grows. With fold weights fixed in advance, the drift terms become weighted averages, which shrink as weight moves toward deployment. The noise term grows as the weights concentrate and shrinks with the batch size. The drift terms are linear in the weights and the noise term is convex, so minimizing the bound over the weights is a convex problem. Applications to U.S. earnings and flight delays show both sides of this trade-off. Weight on recent folds pays off when a change in the best predictor persists and each period has many observations, and equal weights do best when changes are short-lived.
tl_dr: Cross-validation weights all folds equally, so under drift the oldest folds count as much as the newest.

title: Say Less, Hallucinate Less? Diagnosing and Restoring Object Coverage in Preference-Optimized Vision-Language Models
authors_or_owner: Hansang Lee
summary: Preference optimization (PO) is the standard way to reduce object hallucination in large vision-language models. We find that four public PO checkpoints of LLaVA-1.5-7B also lower object coverage. They name fewer object categories, and their lower hallucination rates bring no significant gain in set-level object F1 on CHAIR. We therefore ask how much of the PO gain the base model can reproduce by stopping earlier. A positive end-of-sequence (EOS) logit bias lets the base model reach the recall of each PO model, and this early stopping alone reproduces 58 to 86 percent of the CHAIRi gain of three checkpoints on two disjoint COCO sets. Writing longer does not bring the lost categories back. Under greedy decoding, a negative EOS bias recovers only 2 to 9 percent of the lost CHAIR recall of these checkpoints, and 94 to 96 percent of the added object mentions repeat categories already named. On CHAIR, the base caption of the same image still names about half of the missed object categories. We therefore propose base-guided object-category restoration, which appends high-confidence base-only categories to the PO caption without training. With thresholds fixed on a development set, it brings three checkpoints within one point of the base recall on a held-out COCO set with a lower distinct-object hallucination rate than the base model. Against the recall-matched base stopping curve, its gain holds for RLAIF-V near the base recall and for RLAIF-V and CHAIR-DPO at an intermediate recall. We will release the code of the recall-controlled evaluation.
tl_dr: Preference optimization (PO) is the standard way to reduce object hallucination in large vision-language models.

title: Represented but misread: Post-training changes how language models read out what they represent
authors_or_owner: Jochen Laubrock
summary: Does post-training change what a language model represents, or how this representation is read out into an answer? We compared linear probes with the models' own answers, analyzed with signal detection theory, in six open-weight base models and their post-trained versions. For judgments of whether German texts were written by a human or an AI, probes and word n-gram classifiers separated the classes well, but the answers did not and often ordered the texts inversely. Post-training lowered the sensitivity of the answers on average ($Δd' = -0.34$ across model families; -0.29 across three prompts). It also changed the use of a stated base rate: Base models shifted their log-odds by less than the stated change in prior odds, most post-trained models by more. In two models with stage-wise checkpoints, the change occurred during supervised fine-tuning, model stitching implicated the early layers, and from mid-depth on internal states at positions after the text, not those of the text, transferred the change between checkpoints. Our corpora cannot be shared, so we add a case reproducible from public data, the truth of negated statements. Here, post-training acted in the opposite direction: Probes decoded truth at or near ceiling in every model, the answers of several base models did not use it, and post-training repaired them; by mid-depth the repair resided at the positions after the statement; below it, the representation of the statement contributed, strongly in one of four models. In a training study, adding 2,000 correctly labeled authorship judgments of news texts to otherwise identical fine-tuning data improved the answers on our newspaper and textbook corpora and inverted them on the chats, where they followed a news-trained probe of the base model. Post-training thus changed how a judgment is read out of what a model represents, and a small training signal can set its direction.
tl_dr: Does post-training change what a language model represents, or how this representation is read out into an answer?

title: The Optimal Sample Complexity of Agnostic PAC Learning for Partial Concept Classes
authors_or_owner: Liang-Yu Zou
summary: Let $\mathcal H\subseteq\{-1,+1,\star\}^{\mathcal X}$ be a partial concept class of finite VC dimension $d$. We construct a deterministic agnostic PAC learner that, for every $\varepsilon,δ\in(0,1)$, uses $O((d+\log(1/δ))/\varepsilon^2)$ i.i.d. examples from an arbitrary distribution $\mathcal D$ over $\mathcal X\times\{-1,+1\}$ and returns a total concept $\hat h:\mathcal X\to\{-1,+1\}$ satisfying $\text{er}_{\mathcal D}(\hat h)\leq \min_{h\in\mathcal H}\text{er}_{\mathcal D}(h)+\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-δ$, where $\text{er}_{\mathcal D}(h)=\mathbb P_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal D}[h(x)\neq y]$. This establishes the optimal sample complexity, matching the lower bound of Alon et al. (FOCS 2021).
tl_dr: Let $\mathcal H\subseteq\{-1,+1,\star\}^{\mathcal X}$ be a partial concept class of finite VC dimension $d$.
